items.title: Spring MVC request flow
items.context: Spring MVC follows the Model-View-Controller pattern. The DispatcherServlet is the front controller: every request goes through it first, and it dispatches to the right handler (controller method), which returns a model + view (or, for REST, a response body directly).

questions.prompt: What role does the DispatcherServlet play in Spring MVC?
choices: It only handles static resources like CSS/JS
It's the front controller that receives requests and dispatches them to the right handler
It stores session data
It replaces the need for controllers entirely
questions.explanation: DispatcherServlet is the single entry point for incoming requests; it consults handler mappings to route each request to the appropriate controller method.

questions.prompt: Which annotation maps a controller method specifically to HTTP GET requests on a given path?
choices: @RequestMapping only
@PathVariable
@GetMapping
@ResponseBody
questions.explanation: @GetMapping is a shortcut for @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET) — cleaner for the common case of binding a method to GET.

items.title: Building a REST endpoint
items.context: A typical REST endpoint combines @RestController (so return values serialize straight to JSON/XML) with @RequestMapping/@GetMapping and returns a ResponseEntity to control status code and body explicitly.

questions.prompt: Why return a ResponseEntity<T> instead of just T from a REST controller method?
choices: It automatically encrypts the response
It disables JSON serialization
It lets you explicitly control the HTTP status code and headers, not just the body
It's required by Java syntax
questions.explanation: ResponseEntity wraps the body together with status code and headers, giving you explicit control (e.g. returning 201 Created or 404 Not Found) instead of always defaulting to 200.

items.title: Global exception handling
items.context: Rather than try/catch in every controller, Spring lets you centralize error handling with @ExceptionHandler methods grouped inside a @ControllerAdvice class, applied globally across controllers.

questions.prompt: Which annotation lets you define exception-handling logic that applies globally across all controllers?
choices: @ResponseStatus
@ControllerAdvice
@Valid
@ExceptionHandler alone, on each controller
questions.explanation: @ControllerAdvice groups @ExceptionHandler methods into one place that Spring applies across every controller, avoiding repeated try/catch boilerplate.

items.title: Spring Security basics
items.context: Spring Security handles authentication (who are you) and authorization (what are you allowed to do). Method-level security can use @PreAuthorize (flexible, supports SpEL expressions) or the simpler, role-only @Secured.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between @PreAuthorize and @Secured?
choices: @Secured supports complex SpEL expressions, @PreAuthorize doesn't
@PreAuthorize only works on controllers, @Secured only on services
@PreAuthorize supports flexible SpEL expressions; @Secured only supports simple role checks
They are exactly equivalent
questions.explanation: @PreAuthorize evaluates a Spring Expression Language (SpEL) condition, so it can express much richer rules than @Secured's plain role-name checks.

questions.prompt: You need an endpoint accessible only to users with the ADMIN role. What's a standard way to enforce that at the method level?
choices: Check request.getHeader("role") manually in every method
Rename the method to include 'admin'
Annotate the method with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") or @Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")
Put the method in a package called admin
questions.explanation: Spring Security's method-level annotations let you declare the access rule right on the method, enforced by the framework before the method body runs — no manual header parsing needed.

items.title: Path variables, request params & status codes
items.context: @PathVariable extracts a value from the URL path itself (e.g. /users/{id}); @RequestParam reads a query-string parameter (e.g. ?page=2). Returning the right HTTP status code (200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found, ...) is part of a well-formed REST response.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
choices: @PathVariable only works with numbers
@RequestParam only works with POST requests
They are interchangeable in every case
@PathVariable reads a value from the URL path; @RequestParam reads a query-string parameter
questions.explanation: @PathVariable binds a segment of the URL path itself (like {id} in /users/{id}), while @RequestParam binds a value from the query string (like ?page=2).

questions.prompt: Which HTTP status code should a REST endpoint typically return after successfully creating a new resource?
choices: 400 Bad Request
204 No Content
200 OK
201 Created
questions.explanation: 201 Created signals that a new resource now exists as a result of the request — conventionally paired with a Location header pointing to it.

items.title: CORS & CSRF
items.context: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) controls whether a browser lets JavaScript on one origin call an API on another. CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) protection guards against a malicious site tricking a logged-in user's browser into making unwanted requests, typically via a per-session token.

questions.prompt: What does CORS configuration control?
choices: Whether a browser permits a script on one origin to call an API hosted on a different origin
Which HTTP methods a load balancer accepts
Which database queries are allowed
Password encryption strength
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser-enforced mechanism: the server declares (via response headers) which other origins are allowed to make cross-origin requests to it.

questions.prompt: What is a standard defense against CSRF attacks?
choices: Disabling HTTPS
Storing passwords in plain text
Allowing all origins via CORS
A unique, unpredictable token that must be submitted with state-changing requests
questions.explanation: A CSRF token, unique per session (or per request), must accompany state-changing requests; since an attacker's site can't read or guess it, it can't forge a valid request on the victim's behalf.

items.title: @RequestBody & @ResponseBody
items.context: @RequestBody deserializes an incoming HTTP request body (typically JSON) into a Java object using a configured message converter. @ResponseBody serializes a method's return value directly into the HTTP response body — implied automatically on every method of an @RestController.

questions.prompt: What does @RequestBody do on a controller method parameter?
choices: Reads a query-string parameter
Reads an HTTP header
Deserializes the incoming HTTP request body into that parameter's Java type
Validates the URL path
questions.explanation: @RequestBody tells Spring to convert the raw request body (e.g. JSON) into the annotated parameter's type using an HttpMessageConverter such as Jackson.

questions.prompt: On a plain @Controller (not @RestController), what does adding @ResponseBody to a method achieve?
choices: It makes the method private
It serializes the method's return value straight into the response body instead of resolving it as a view name
It disables the method entirely
It forces the response to always be XML
questions.explanation: Without @ResponseBody, a @Controller method's return value is normally treated as a view name to render; @ResponseBody bypasses view resolution and writes the return value directly to the response body.

items.title: Request validation with @Valid
items.context: Annotating a @RequestBody parameter with @Valid triggers Bean Validation (JSR 380) against constraint annotations on the target class, like @NotNull, @Size, and @Email — invalid requests are rejected with a 400 before the handler method body even runs.

questions.prompt: Which annotation, applied to a @RequestBody parameter, triggers Bean Validation constraints declared on that class?
choices: @Validated
@Constraint
@Check
@Valid
questions.explanation: @Valid on a @RequestBody parameter tells Spring to run Bean Validation against the incoming object's constraint annotations (@NotNull, @Size, etc.) before the handler method executes.

items.title: HTTP method idempotency
items.context: An idempotent HTTP method produces the same server state no matter how many times an identical request is repeated. GET, PUT, and DELETE are meant to be idempotent; POST is not — repeating it can create multiple resources.

questions.prompt: Which of these HTTP methods is NOT expected to be idempotent?
choices: PUT
POST
GET
DELETE
questions.explanation: POST is defined as non-idempotent: submitting the same POST request twice can (and often does) create two separate resources, unlike GET/PUT/DELETE which should leave the server in the same state if repeated.

items.title: Filters vs Interceptors
items.context: A Servlet Filter operates at the servlet-container level, before a request even reaches Spring's DispatcherServlet — useful for concerns like logging or CORS that apply to every request regardless of framework. A Spring HandlerInterceptor runs inside the Spring MVC request-handling flow and has access to the specific handler being invoked.

questions.prompt: What's a key difference between a Servlet Filter and a Spring HandlerInterceptor?
choices: Filters can only be used with REST APIs, never with Spring MVC views
Interceptors can only run after the response is sent
A Filter runs at the servlet-container level before Spring's DispatcherServlet; an Interceptor runs inside Spring MVC with access to the specific handler
They are exactly the same mechanism
questions.explanation: Filters are part of the Servlet spec and see every request/response passing through the container, framework-agnostic; Interceptors are Spring MVC-specific and plug into the DispatcherServlet's own handling pipeline, with visibility into which controller method will handle the request.

items.title: Content negotiation
items.context: A client signals the response format it wants via the Accept header (e.g. application/json). Spring MVC's message converters use this to decide how to serialize the response body, letting the same endpoint serve JSON or XML depending on what's requested.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP request header does a client use to indicate which response format (e.g. JSON vs XML) it prefers?
choices: Authorization
Accept
Cache-Control
Content-Type
questions.explanation: Accept tells the server which media type(s) the client can handle for the response; Content-Type instead describes the media type of the request body being sent.

items.title: @ModelAttribute
items.context: @ModelAttribute binds request parameters onto a Java object's fields automatically (commonly for form submissions), and can also be used on a method to add common data to the model for every handler in a controller.

questions.prompt: What does @ModelAttribute on a controller method parameter typically do?
choices: Reads a single request header
Forces the response to be JSON
Binds matching request parameters onto the fields of the given object automatically
Rejects the request if validation fails, with no further behavior
questions.explanation: @ModelAttribute populates an object's fields from request parameters with matching names — commonly used to bind an HTML form submission directly onto a Java object without manual parameter-by-parameter extraction.

items.title: Serving static resources
items.context: Spring Boot automatically serves static content (HTML, CSS, JS, images) placed in specific classpath locations — most commonly src/main/resources/static — without any extra controller code.

questions.prompt: Where would you place a static index.html file so Spring Boot serves it automatically, with no extra configuration?
choices: target/classes/controllers
src/main/java
src/test/resources
src/main/resources/static
questions.explanation: Spring Boot's default static-resource handling looks in classpath locations including /static, /public, /resources, and /META-INF/resources — src/main/resources/static is the most commonly used of these.

items.title: WebSockets
items.context: Unlike a typical HTTP request/response cycle, a WebSocket connection stays open, allowing full-duplex, bidirectional messaging between client and server — well suited to real-time features like chat or live notifications.

questions.prompt: What fundamentally distinguishes a WebSocket connection from a typical HTTP request/response?
choices: WebSockets can only send data from server to client
A WebSocket connection stays open for full-duplex, bidirectional messaging, instead of one request producing one response
WebSockets don't require a network connection
WebSockets are just a faster version of HTTP GET
questions.explanation: Once established, a WebSocket connection remains open and lets either side push messages to the other at any time, unlike HTTP's request-then-response model which closes (or at best keeps-alive) after each exchange.

items.title: Multipart file uploads
items.context: A Spring MVC controller accepts an uploaded file by declaring a MultipartFile parameter, which exposes the file's bytes, original filename, and content type.

questions.prompt: Which type does a Spring MVC controller method use to receive an uploaded file?
choices: MultipartFile
byte[]
File
InputStream only, with no metadata
questions.explanation: MultipartFile represents an uploaded file from a multipart/form-data request, giving access to its content, original filename, size, and content type in one object.

items.title: @ResponseStatus
items.context: @ResponseStatus declaratively sets the HTTP status code returned for a specific exception class or handler method, instead of setting it manually on a ResponseEntity every time.

questions.prompt: What does annotating a custom exception class with @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) achieve?
choices: It prevents the exception from ever being thrown
It logs the exception with 'NOT_FOUND' severity
When that exception is thrown and reaches Spring's default handling, the response automatically gets a 404 status
It only affects unit tests, not real requests
questions.explanation: @ResponseStatus lets you declare the HTTP status that should accompany a given exception (or handler method) once, on the class itself, instead of manually building a ResponseEntity with that status everywhere it might be thrown.

items.title: Asynchronous request handling
items.context: Returning a Callable<T> or DeferredResult<T> from a controller method frees up the servlet container's request-handling thread while a long-running operation completes elsewhere, letting the container serve other requests in the meantime instead of blocking a thread per slow request.

questions.prompt: What's the main benefit of returning a Callable or DeferredResult from a Spring MVC controller method for a slow operation?
choices: It disables timeouts entirely
It makes the operation itself run faster
It automatically retries the operation on failure
It frees the servlet container's request thread while the slow work completes elsewhere, improving overall throughput
questions.explanation: Async return types release the container thread that received the request back to the pool while the actual work happens on another thread (or callback), so that thread can go serve other incoming requests instead of sitting blocked — improving throughput under many concurrent slow requests.

items.title: Spring Boot Actuator
items.context: Spring Boot Actuator exposes production-ready endpoints out of the box for monitoring and managing a running application — health status, metrics, environment info, and more — without writing that infrastructure yourself.

questions.prompt: What does adding Spring Boot Actuator to a project primarily provide?
choices: Automatic database schema migration
A new templating engine
A built-in front-end framework
Production-ready endpoints for monitoring/managing the app, like health checks and metrics
questions.explanation: Actuator adds ready-made operational endpoints (health, info, metrics, env, and more) that ops tooling and load balancers commonly poll, without you having to build that monitoring surface by hand.

questions.prompt: Which default Actuator endpoint reports whether the application is up and its dependencies (like the database) are reachable?
choices: /actuator/loggers
/actuator/mappings
/actuator/beans
/actuator/health
questions.explanation: /actuator/health is the standard endpoint load balancers and orchestration systems (like Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes) poll to decide whether an instance is healthy.

items.title: Authentication approaches
items.context: HTTP Basic Auth sends credentials (base64-encoded, not encrypted) with every single request and has no built-in way to expire or revoke access short of changing the password. Token-based approaches (like JWTs) instead issue a time-limited token after login, which is then presented on each request and can be revoked or allowed to expire independently of the user's actual password.

questions.prompt: What is a key weakness of HTTP Basic Authentication compared to token-based authentication?
choices: It cannot be used over HTTPS
It only works with GET requests
Credentials are sent with every request and there's no built-in way to expire or revoke access without changing the password
It requires a database
questions.explanation: Basic Auth resends the actual username/password on every request with no separate, revocable session concept — compromising a request exposes the real credentials, and there's no way to invalidate just one session without changing the password for everyone using it.

items.title: @ExceptionHandler return values
items.context: An @ExceptionHandler method isn't limited to returning a view name or a plain string — it can return a ResponseEntity<T> to fully control the status code, headers, and a structured error body, which is the standard approach for REST APIs.

questions.prompt: Can an @ExceptionHandler method return a ResponseEntity with a custom JSON error body and specific status code?
choices: Yes — returning a ResponseEntity gives full control over status code, headers, and a structured error body
Only if the method is also annotated @Deprecated
No, @ExceptionHandler can only return void
Only for 500-level errors
questions.explanation: @ExceptionHandler methods behave like any other handler method — returning a ResponseEntity lets you shape a proper structured error response (status, headers, JSON body) instead of a bare message.

items.title: OAuth2 vs JWT vs Basic Auth
items.context: OAuth2 is an authorization framework/protocol for delegated access (letting an app act on a user's behalf without seeing their password). JWT is a token format — a compact, signed way to carry claims — often used as the access token inside an OAuth2 flow, but usable standalone too. Basic Auth simply sends the raw username/password (base64-encoded, not encrypted) on every request.

questions.prompt: What's the relationship between OAuth2 and JWT?
choices: JWT replaces the need for OAuth2 entirely
OAuth2 only works without any tokens
OAuth2 is an authorization framework for delegated access; JWT is a token format often used to carry the access tokens within an OAuth2 flow
They are two names for the exact same thing
questions.explanation: OAuth2 defines the flows and roles for delegated authorization (who grants access, how tokens are obtained); JWT is a specific, self-contained token format that's commonly (but not exclusively) used to represent the tokens OAuth2 issues.

items.title: Transport security vs application-level security
items.context: HTTPS/TLS secures the transport — encrypting data in transit and helping verify the server's identity — but it doesn't by itself authenticate a specific user or authorize what they're allowed to do. Those responsibilities still sit with the application (Spring Security, in a Spring app).

questions.prompt: Does enabling HTTPS on an API endpoint by itself authenticate who is calling it?
choices: HTTPS replaces the need for any login system
Yes, HTTPS handles authentication and authorization completely
No — HTTPS encrypts the connection and verifies the server's identity, but the application still needs its own authentication/authorization (e.g. Spring Security)
HTTPS is only about compressing traffic
questions.explanation: HTTPS protects data in transit from eavesdropping/tampering and confirms you're talking to the right server, but it says nothing about who the caller is or what they're permitted to do — that's a separate, application-level concern.

items.title: The Spring Security filter chain
items.context: Spring Security enforces authentication and authorization through a chain of servlet Filters that run before a request reaches the DispatcherServlet — each filter handles one concern (e.g. one type of authentication, CSRF checking, exception translation) and can short-circuit the request before it ever reaches a controller.

questions.prompt: How does Spring Security typically intercept and secure incoming requests?
choices: By modifying the compiled bytecode of controllers
Only through database triggers
By wrapping every controller method in a try/catch
Through a chain of servlet Filters that run before the request reaches the DispatcherServlet, each handling one security concern
questions.explanation: Spring Security installs a chain of Filters ahead of the DispatcherServlet in the servlet container's filter pipeline — authentication, CSRF protection, exception handling, and authorization checks each typically live in their own filter, composed together.

items.title: @CrossOrigin for per-endpoint CORS
items.context: @CrossOrigin, placed on a controller or handler method, enables CORS for just that endpoint declaratively — a lighter-weight alternative to configuring CORS globally for the whole application.

questions.prompt: What does adding @CrossOrigin to a single controller method do?
choices: Enables CORS specifically for that endpoint, without needing global CORS configuration
Disables CORS checks application-wide
Encrypts that endpoint's responses
Forces that endpoint to require authentication
questions.explanation: @CrossOrigin is a targeted, per-endpoint way to opt into CORS, useful when only specific endpoints need to be called from a different origin rather than the whole API.

items.title: CSRF and stateless APIs
items.context: CSRF protection defends against a malicious site tricking a logged-in browser (using cookies/sessions) into making unwanted requests. A stateless REST API authenticated via a bearer token (not cookies) generally disables CSRF protection, since there's no ambient browser session for another site to piggyback on.

questions.prompt: Why is CSRF protection commonly disabled for a stateless, token-authenticated REST API?
choices: Without cookie/session-based auth, there's no ambient browser credential for another site to silently reuse, removing the attack CSRF protection defends against
REST APIs are immune to all attacks by design
Disabling CSRF makes the API faster
CSRF is impossible to defend against for APIs
questions.explanation: CSRF exploits the browser automatically attaching session cookies to requests; a stateless API using an explicit bearer token (sent deliberately by the calling code, not auto-attached by the browser) isn't vulnerable to that particular attack in the same way, so many stateless APIs disable CSRF protection.

items.title: URL-based vs method-level security
items.context: Spring Security can restrict access by URL pattern (configured on the HttpSecurity chain, e.g. "/admin/**" requires ADMIN role) and/or by method (via @PreAuthorize on individual service or controller methods) — the two can be combined, with method-level security offering finer-grained control than URL patterns alone.

questions.prompt: What's an advantage of method-level security (@PreAuthorize) over relying solely on URL-pattern security rules?
choices: URL-pattern security cannot be combined with method-level security
Method-level security doesn't require Spring Security
Method-level security is always faster
It offers finer-grained control, since a rule can depend on the specific method's arguments or return value, not just the URL
questions.explanation: URL patterns can only key off the path being requested; @PreAuthorize can express conditions based on the actual method's parameters or even the returned object (via @PostAuthorize), enabling rules URL matching alone can't express.

items.title: ResponseEntity convenience methods
items.context: Static helpers like ResponseEntity.ok(body), .notFound().build(), and .status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(x) provide shorter, more readable alternatives to the full ResponseEntity constructor for common response shapes.

questions.prompt: What does ResponseEntity.notFound().build() produce?
choices: A 500 Internal Server Error
A 200 OK response with an empty body
A 404 Not Found response with no body
A compile error — build() doesn't exist
questions.explanation: ResponseEntity.notFound() starts a builder pre-set to a 404 status, and build() finalizes it with no body — a concise way to express a common 'nothing found' response.

items.title: Constraining @PathVariable format
items.context: A path pattern like /users/{id:[0-9]+} constrains what the {id} segment can match directly in the mapping — requests where that segment isn't purely digits won't match this handler at all, rather than matching and then failing type conversion.

questions.prompt: What does writing @GetMapping("/users/{id:[0-9]+}") achieve compared to a plain {id}?
choices: It disables path variable binding entirely
It converts id to a String automatically
Nothing different — the regex is ignored
It restricts matching to paths where id is purely digits, so non-numeric values won't even route to this handler
questions.explanation: Embedding a regex constraint directly in the path pattern filters which requests match this handler at the routing level itself, rather than matching broadly and discovering a type-conversion failure later inside the method.

items.title: Digest authentication
items.context: HTTP Digest authentication hashes the credentials together with a server-provided nonce before sending them, rather than transmitting them in a merely base64-encoded (not encrypted) form the way Basic Auth does — though in modern practice, token-based auth over HTTPS has mostly superseded both.

questions.prompt: How does Digest authentication improve on Basic authentication's handling of credentials?
choices: It doesn't — they are identical
It requires no server-side verification at all
It hashes the credentials with a server-provided nonce instead of sending them in an easily-decoded base64 form
It only works over unencrypted HTTP
questions.explanation: Digest auth avoids sending the actual password (even encoded) over the wire by combining it with a nonce and hashing before transmission — a meaningful improvement over Basic Auth's plainly-decodable credentials, though both are largely superseded by modern token-based schemes over HTTPS today.

items.title: Custom HandlerMethodArgumentResolver
items.context: Implementing HandlerMethodArgumentResolver lets you teach Spring MVC how to automatically resolve a custom parameter type on controller methods (e.g. a @CurrentUser annotation that resolves to the logged-in user object), instead of manually extracting it from the request in every handler.

questions.prompt: What does implementing a custom HandlerMethodArgumentResolver let you do?
choices: Bypass Spring Security entirely
Teach Spring MVC how to automatically supply a custom parameter type to controller methods, based on your own resolution logic
Add new REST endpoints without a controller class
Change the HTTP method a controller responds to
questions.explanation: A custom HandlerMethodArgumentResolver plugs into Spring MVC's parameter-binding process, letting you define once how to produce a value for a particular parameter type/annotation — reused automatically across every controller method that declares it, instead of duplicating extraction logic everywhere.

items.title: Wrong Content-Type on @RequestBody

questions.prompt: What happens to this request?
choices: 200 OK, with an empty User
Spring parses the body as JSON anyway
The request fails with 415 Unsupported Media Type (HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException)
user is bound with all fields null
questions.explanation: @RequestBody relies on Spring's HttpMessageConverters to pick a converter based on the request's declared Content-Type. text/plain doesn't match any converter capable of producing a User object (normally MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter expects application/json), so Spring throws HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException, translated to a 415 response — before your controller code even runs.

items.title: @PathVariable type mismatch

questions.prompt: What happens to this request?
choices: 404 Not Found
400 Bad Request via MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException
500 Internal Server Error with a NumberFormatException in the response body
id is bound to 0
questions.explanation: Spring tries to convert the path segment "abc" to an int to bind @PathVariable id. That conversion fails, and Spring wraps it in MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException, which by default maps to a 400 Bad Request — treated as a client error (a malformed request), not a server bug, even though the root cause is a NumberFormatException-style failure.

items.title: @Valid failing on a @RequestBody

questions.prompt: What happens to this request?
choices: 400 Bad Request via MethodArgumentNotValidException, listing both violations
Only the first violation (@NotBlank) is reported; validation stops there
200 OK — bean validation isn't checked unless explicitly called
500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: @Valid on a @RequestBody parameter triggers Spring's bean validation immediately after binding. Any constraint violations are collected into a BindingResult and, since the controller method here doesn't declare a BindingResult parameter to handle them manually, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException — mapped by default to 400, with the response body normally listing all failed constraints, not just the first one.

items.title: ConstraintViolationException on a @RequestParam

questions.prompt: What is thrown, and what HTTP status does it map to by default?
choices: ConstraintViolationException, 500 (no default handler registers it as 400)
MethodArgumentNotValidException, 400
MissingServletRequestParameterException, 400
Nothing — @Size is silently ignored on @RequestParam
questions.explanation: Method-level constraints on individual @RequestParam/@PathVariable arguments (enabled by class-level @Validated) are validated by a different mechanism than @Valid @RequestBody — they throw ConstraintViolationException, not MethodArgumentNotValidException. Unlike the RequestBody case, Spring MVC has no built-in default handler that maps ConstraintViolationException to 400, so — surprisingly — it falls through to a plain 500 Internal Server Error unless you add your own @ExceptionHandler for it.

items.title: Missing a required @RequestParam

questions.prompt: What happens to this request?
choices: q is bound to null, and the method runs normally
400 Bad Request via MissingServletRequestParameterException
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: @RequestParam parameters are required by default (required = true). If the client omits the parameter entirely, Spring throws MissingServletRequestParameterException before invoking the controller method, mapped to a 400 response. Making it optional requires either required = false or giving it a default value.

items.title: Duplicate @GetMapping paths

questions.prompt: What happens when the Spring application context starts up with these two mappings?
choices: Both are registered; Spring picks whichever matches first at request time
Only the first-declared method is registered; the second is ignored
A 500 error occurs the first time the endpoint is actually called
Context startup fails with an IllegalStateException about an ambiguous mapping
questions.explanation: Two handler methods mapped to the exact same path and HTTP method (with nothing else to disambiguate, like different `params` or `produces`) is detected at startup, not at request time — Spring throws an IllegalStateException ("Ambiguous mapping") while building the request-mapping registry, so the application never even finishes starting.

items.title: Missing CSRF token on a state-changing request
items.context:
http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.csrfTokenRepository(...)); // CSRF protection enabled (Spring default for stateful apps)

// Client sends: POST /transfer  (no X-CSRF-TOKEN header, no _csrf param)

questions.prompt: What happens to this request?
choices: The request succeeds but is logged as suspicious
403 Forbidden — the CSRF token is missing or invalid
200 OK — CSRF only applies to GET requests
401 Unauthorized
questions.explanation: Spring Security's CSRF protection requires state-changing requests (POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH by default) to include a valid CSRF token matching the one issued to that session. A POST with no token at all is rejected by the CsrfFilter before it ever reaches the controller, returning 403 Forbidden — distinct from 401, which specifically means "you're not authenticated at all".

items.title: 403 vs 401 with @PreAuthorize

questions.prompt: What HTTP status is returned, and why is it not 401?
choices: 401 Unauthorized, because the check failed
403 Forbidden — the user IS authenticated, just lacks the required authority; 401 is reserved for missing/invalid credentials
404 Not Found, to avoid leaking the endpoint's existence
500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized means "who are you? — authentication itself failed or is missing." 403 Forbidden means "I know who you are, and you're not allowed to do this." Here the user successfully authenticated but their granted authorities don't satisfy hasRole('ADMIN'), so @PreAuthorize's access-denied path correctly results in 403, not 401 — a distinction that's easy to get backwards.

items.title: Unknown JSON field with default Jackson settings

questions.prompt: What happens to this request?
choices: unexpectedField is silently added to the DTO as a dynamic property
400 Bad Request via HttpMessageNotReadableException, because of the unrecognized field
500 Internal Server Error
Ignores unexpectedField and binds name normally — 200 OK
questions.explanation: Jackson's FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is true by default, so deserializing JSON containing a field the target DTO doesn't declare throws an UnrecognizedPropertyException, which Spring's message converter wraps as HttpMessageNotReadableException — mapped to 400 Bad Request. (Note: many Spring Boot setups explicitly disable this Jackson feature for a more lenient API, so real behavior always depends on configuration — but the unconfigured default is strict.)

items.title: Unhandled RuntimeException defaults to 500

questions.prompt: What HTTP status does the client see when the widget isn't found?
choices: 500 Internal Server Error — an unhandled RuntimeException always defaults to 500
204 No Content
404 Not Found, since Spring infers this from the exception message
400 Bad Request
questions.explanation: Spring MVC's default behavior for any uncaught exception that isn't specifically mapped (via @ResponseStatus on the exception class, a @ExceptionHandler, or a recognized Spring MVC exception type) is to respond with 500 Internal Server Error. A plain `throw new RuntimeException("not found")` carries no information telling Spring this should be a 404 — you'd need a custom exception annotated @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND), or an explicit handler, to get that semantically correct response.
